title: Beshalach: stop praying, move (Exodus 14:15)
hook: at the sea, God asks Moses why he cries out, and tells the people to go forward

segments.voice: Yesterday Moses packed Joseph's bones while everyone else packed silver. Your line was carry the bones. Did you take a step on an old promise? Today, the sea in front of them, and an army behind. Day three hundred forty.

An email drafted and never sent. A doctor's appointment someone keeps meaning to book. A thing gets thought about, worried about, maybe prayed about, until the thinking itself becomes a place to hide. The Israelites are trapped. The sea is in front of them, and Pharaoh's chariots are coming up behind. The people cry out in terror. Moses tells them to stand still and watch. And then God says something to Moses that sounds, at first, almost like a rebuke.
screen: `THE EMAIL YOU NEVER SEND.` → `SEA IN FRONT, CHARIOTS BEHIND.` → `GOD SPEAKS TO MOSES.`

segments.voice: God asks Moses why he is crying out. Then: "speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Here's the strange part. The Torah never shows Moses crying out. The people cried out, a few verses earlier. Moses told them to be calm. So what is God answering? Rashi, the medieval commentator, says the verse teaches that Moses was standing and praying, silently, and God's reply means: this is not the time for long prayer. Israel is in danger. Move. It isn't that prayer is wrong. Moses prayed many times, and God listened. It's that prayer has a time, and so does walking. The rabbis then tell a story about who took the first step. In the Talmud, Rabbi Judah says the tribes stood at the shore, each wanting someone else to go first. Then Nachshon, son of Amminadav, of the tribe of Judah, jumped into the water. In some tellings, he waded in until it reached his neck, and only then did the sea split. That's midrash, a story the tradition tells about the gap between one verse and the next. The Torah itself simply says Moses lifted his rod, stretched his hand over the sea, and a strong east wind blew all night. The story keeps being told for the picture it leaves: the sea parting in front of someone who is already walking.
screen: `WHY DO YOU CRY OUT TO ME?` · `RASHI: NOT THE TIME FOR LONG PRAYER.` · `NACHSHON STEPS IN FIRST.` · `THE STRONG EAST WIND.` · then, large: `PRAY, THEN GO FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the sea in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been circling. You've thought about it enough. If you pray, pray about it now, briefly and honestly. If you don't, just name it clearly to yourself. Then picture the very first step. Not the whole crossing. One step: the first sentence of the email, the phone number dialed, the shoes put on. See your foot touching the water. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where at the edge of the sea God tells Moses: speak to the people, and let them go forward.
Your line: pray, then go forward. Today, take the first step on the thing you've been circling, right after you finish thinking about it. Day three hundred forty.

screen: `DAY 340 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BESHALACH: BITTER WATER MADE SWEET (EXODUS 15:22–26).`

howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue twice a year: in the weekly portion Beshalach, and on the seventh day of Passover, which tradition dates to the night of the crossing. Nachshon is taught to children as the one who stepped in first.

options: keep praying until the sea opens.
speak to the people, that they go forward.

fork.reveal: go forward. Rashi reads it: this is not the time for long prayer. Israel is in danger. move.

original.note: Hebrew: and let them journey on, go forward. from the verb for breaking camp and setting out.

trapdoor: what you thought: God tells Moses to stop praying.
what it means: prayer has its time, and so does moving; at the sea, it's time to move.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 14:15 infers a silent prayer the text never shows; Sotah 37a tells of Nachshon of Judah entering the sea first.
